notes.meaning: David begins his song by pleading with God to pay attention to his prayer. He feels as though God might be hiding or turning His face away from his urgent cry. In deep sorrow, God's people naturally turn straight to Him for relief.

David is restless and cannot hold back his groans. His mind wanders through heavy grief, and he lets out noisy cries of sorrow. Believers are free to bring even their confused and distracted complaints directly to God.

The king is distressed because his enemies are shouting threats and pressing down on him. They make up terrible lies about him to convince the public that he deserves ruin. Their deep hatred has no good reason, yet it burns with violent anger.

David feels sharp agony deep in his chest, like the pains of childbirth. The dread of death falls over him like a dark shadow. Even the bravest servants of God can feel their courage give way in severe trials.

Violent shaking and intense fear take hold of David's whole body. A deep sense of horror rolls over him and leaves him feeling stunned. These words honestly describe the panic that strikes someone facing sudden ruin.

David wishes he had wings like a dove so he could quickly fly away to safety. A dove is gentle and flies swiftly to high rocks when a hawk attacks. Instead of seeking revenge or victory, the king simply longs for quiet rest.

David pictures himself escaping far away to live alone in the barren wilderness. In his grief, an empty desert seems far safer and more peaceful than his rebellious royal city. He pauses to let his troubled mind rest before God.

David wants to rush to shelter before the coming storm tears everything apart. He compares the raging uprising against him to a violent windstorm. His great desire is to escape the noise and chaos around him.

David asks the Lord to confuse the speech and plans of his foes, just as God once scattered the proud builders at Babel. He sees that Jerusalem is full of open fighting and cruelty. God answered this cry when the conspirators began arguing over what strategy to follow.

Cruelty and quarreling seem to walk along the city walls day and night like armed guards. Inside the streets, people suffer from constant trouble, grief, and crime. A city once devoted to God has been taken over by lawlessness.

Destruction fills the center of the town, while lying and cheating never leave the public squares. The open plazas were meant for fair business and just judges, but evil men have ruined them. The public life of the whole nation has become thoroughly corrupted.

The hardest part of David's trial is that the insult comes from an insider, not a declared enemy. A person can prepare for an attack from a known rival, or hide from it. Treachery from someone you trusted cuts far deeper because it takes you by surprise.

David points out that the traitor was his equal in standing, a trusted guide, and a close friend. This refers especially to his wise counselor Ahithophel, whose advice the king trusted completely. It shows how terrible it is when a trusted companion breaks faith.

David remembers how they shared their innermost thoughts and walked together in the crowds going to God's house. Their friendship was not just about politics, but was sealed by worshipping the Lord together. Using religion as a mask for betrayal makes the treachery far worse.

David asks that sudden death catch the rebels by surprise and drag them alive into Sheol, the place of the dead, just as happened to Korah long ago. This severe prayer announces God's sure judgment on those who rebel against His chosen king. Evil has made its home inside their houses and deep in their hearts.

While his enemies rely on deceit and violence, David resolves to call on God. He is completely sure that the Lord will rescue him from danger. A believer finds true peace by handing the problem over to God.

David sets aside regular times to pray three times a day—evening, morning, and noon. He cries out from the heart, confident that the Lord will listen to his voice. Meeting hardship with steady prayer keeps our faith strong throughout the day.

God rescues David's soul and gives him inward peace, even while a great battle rages around him. Faith allows the king to speak of his rescue as already accomplished. He knows that God's heavenly helpers and faithful friends outnumber all who fight against him.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine applied the words about those who were 'with me' to heretics who share the church's sacraments but do not share genuine love.

notes.meaning: The eternal God, who has ruled as King from ancient days, will hear David's cry and bring low his proud enemies. These wicked men have no fear of God because their lives have been easy and free of trouble. Unbroken prosperity often blinds sinners to their true spiritual danger.

The traitor attacks the very people who lived in peace with him and did him no harm. He shamelessly breaks his solemn promises and treaties of loyalty. Striking a trusting friend who suspects nothing is deeply wicked.

The traitor's words sounded smoother than butter and softer than olive oil, but his heart was planning war. His flattering speech was only a disguise to hide deadly, drawn swords. Believers must be careful not to trust people whose sweet talk hides harmful intentions.

David urges everyone who is troubled to roll their heavy burdens and worries onto the Lord. God promises to provide food and strength to sustain His people through every storm. He will never allow those who trust Him to be permanently ruined.

differ.view: This promise means that God will never allow true believers to fall away completely or lose their salvation.
God will keep believers from being completely crushed by trials, though He may permit them to be shaken for a time.

notes.meaning: God will bring violent and deceitful plotters down into the dark pit of destruction. Men who live by bloodshed and trickery will often have their lives cut short by an early, violent death under divine justice. Meanwhile, David ends his song by quietly placing all his trust in God.
